h1: Spot the scam before it costs you.
lead: GLOPROFAS helps individuals, families and businesses recognise fraud, protect their money and know what to do next. Start with a free guide, or report what happened to you.
strip: Got a suspicious message? Check before you pay.
introH2: Fighting scams through awareness, prevention and action.
introBody: The Global Programme for the Fight Against Scams is an independent, not-for-profit initiative. Scams move fast across borders and phones; clear information moves slower. We close that gap by turning what people report into warnings anyone can act on, with particular attention to Africa and Cameroon.
outreachH2: Campaigns, seminars and forums where people already gather.
outreachLead: GLOPROFAS leads anti-scam campaigns, seminars and forums in schools, churches, youth centres and companies. The sessions sensitise people to the threats, risks and consequences of every kind of fraud, with a particular focus on modern-day scamming schemes.

places.title: Schools
places.text: Classroom seminars that name the tricks before a fee, a code or a fake job offer reaches a student.

places.title: Churches
places.text: Forums for congregations on impersonation, charity appeals and pressure to pay in secret.

places.title: Youth centres
places.text: Workshops on social-media scams, mobile money and the right to pause before sending anything.

places.title: Companies
places.text: Seminars for staff on invoice swaps, phishing and the cost of a culture that forbids a question.

loginLead: Reports, alerts and settings. This is not a public account.
loginHint: Change this password before a real launch.
checks: Written for everyday people, not specialists
Warnings drawn from real public reports
Help for households, businesses and communities
A global mission, rooted in African realities
scamsH2: Know the tricks people use most.
scamsLead: Each guide explains how the scam works, the warning signs and what to do if it happens to you.
howH2: Most scams follow the same four moves.

steps.title: Contact
steps.text: A message, call or post arrives, often looking official or friendly.

steps.title: Pressure
steps.text: Urgency, fear or a great opportunity pushes you to act now.

steps.title: Payment
steps.text: You are asked to pay, transfer or share a code.

steps.title: Disappearance
steps.text: The contact goes silent and the money is gone.

techniqueItems.title: Psychological manipulation
techniqueItems.text: Playing on trust, fear, hope or shame so you stop questioning.

techniqueItems.title: Fake identities
techniqueItems.text: Stolen photos, invented profiles and borrowed names.

techniqueItems.title: Urgency and intimidation
techniqueItems.text: Deadlines, threats of blocked accounts or legal trouble.

techniqueItems.title: Fake investment opportunities
techniqueItems.text: Guaranteed returns, early “winners” and pressure to recruit.

techniqueItems.title: Impersonation
techniqueItems.text: Posing as a relative, a bank, an operator or an official.

techniqueItems.title: Social engineering
techniqueItems.text: Gathering small details to make a later request believable.

techniqueItems.title: Fraudulent payment requests
techniqueItems.text: Fake invoices, changed bank details and reversal requests.

techniqueItems.title: Fake websites and applications
techniqueItems.text: Copycat pages and apps built to take payments or logins.

servicesH2: Free for the public. Professional support when you need more.
freeBody: Awareness pages, alerts, the reporting channel and general guidance are free. They do not create a client relationship.
paidBody: Assessments, training and advisory work are separate, optional and priced only when an administrator sets a mode. We do not invent fees.

finalH2: Together, we can make the digital world safer.
finalLead: Report what you saw, read the guidance, or write to the team.

footerDisclaimer: GLOPROFAS is not a government body or law enforcement authority, cannot guarantee recovery of funds and does not certify any website or person as legitimate. Contact your financial institution and the competent authorities through official channels.

report.nextBody: Authorised staff may review the report. We may email you if more information is needed. We will not contact you on a random messaging app and ask for codes or further payments.

report.safetyBody: Contact your bank or mobile-money provider using the number on your card, app or receipt. Do not use a number that arrived inside the suspicious message.

pillarsLead: Three pillars, one goal: fewer people paying scammers.

pillars.title: Real-time Database Check
pillars.desc: Before you act, the assistant cross-checks a suspicious message against GLOPROFAS's live database of published scam patterns and alerts. It gives guidance only and never certifies anyone as legitimate.

pillars.title: Community Reporting
pillars.desc: Private, no-account reports from people on the ground are reviewed by authorised staff and, once approved, become anonymised public alerts that protect the next person.

pillars.title: Secure Analytics
pillars.desc: Report trends are analysed privately to show where the next wave of fraud is heading. Your information is never sold and never published.

support.lead: You are not to blame. These guides walk through the immediate protective actions for the situations people report most often. None of them promise that money can be recovered.
support.intro: Choose your situation below. Each guide explains what to do first, what to preserve, and where to turn — through official channels you verify yourself.

situations.t: Money sent to a suspected scammer
situations.d: Contact your bank or mobile-money operator now through its official channel. Keep the messages, receipts and numbers involved.

situations.t: My mobile-money account may be compromised
situations.d: Change your PIN, review your statement for unfamiliar entries and contact the operator through a channel you verify yourself.

situations.t: I shared a password or one-time code
situations.d: Change that password from a device you trust, sign out of other sessions, and switch on two-factor authentication where the service offers it.
Do not enter any details on that page. Change any password you may have typed and check your recent transactions.
Uninstall it, run a scan where possible and change any passwords you may have typed into it.
Watch for unexpected accounts or credit in your name and contact the affected institutions through official channels.
Call your provider on its official number to restore service, and warn the people closest to you.

situations.t: I am being threatened or blackmailed
situations.d: Do not pay. Keep the messages as evidence and, if you feel unsafe, contact local authorities through official channels.

situations.t: A fake investment asked for more money
situations.d: Stop sending money. Check any named operator with your country’s regulator through official channels.

situations.t: A social-media account was taken over
situations.d: Use the platform’s recovery process to regain it and warn your contacts that it was misused.
Before paying, confirm the payment details by a phone number you already had. Never rely on the email alone.

situations.t: Someone offered to “recover” my lost money
situations.d: Recovery offers are very often a second scam. Use only the original provider’s official channels.

assess.title: Indicative check
assess.note: Indicative only. This does not prove the message is, or is not, a scam.
assess.warning: Before pasting any message, remove passwords, PINs, one-time codes, full card numbers and identity numbers.
